articles.title: Resources minister faces calls to correct her claim all Beetaloo emissions will be offset
articles.summary: Madeleine King told press club emissions from NT fossil fuel basin ‘are accounted for and offset’ but research found 95% of emissions this decade would not have to be offset
articles.byline: Adam Morton and Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: The resources minister, Madeleine King, is facing calls to correct her claim in a major speech that all greenhouse gas emissions from developing a massive fossil fuel basin in the Northern Territory will be offset to limit their impact on the climate.

Speaking at the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday, King defended her support for the development of the Beetaloo gas basin south of Darwin after being asked if she was comfortable with the impact that the emissions from the gas would have on Australians.

King was photographed laughing alongside the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, as they celebrated the first gas being pumped from the basin last month. The minister told the press club the basin was a “very important resource” for the NT and to help supply gas to Australia’s east coast and export markets.

She said it was being developed after a “landmark scientific study” in 2018 into whether fracking should be allowed in the territory. Known as the Pepper inquiry, that government-commissioned investigation made 135 recommendations, including that the NT and Australian governments should aim to ensure that any onshore shale gas developments did not increase the country’s total emissions.
In practice, that would require any climate pollution from gas developments – from extraction, processing, transport and the fuel’s use – to be fully offset through the purchase of carbon credits.

King told the press club that the NT government “took up and implemented” the inquiry’s recommendations. “My understanding from those recommendations is that the emissions are accounted for and offset, but I would have to check that,” she said.

The NT government does not require emissions from Beetaloo basin to be offset. The Guardian revealed that the previous Labor territory government dropped the requirement after the gas industry objected. The Country Liberal party government maintained that position when elected in 2024.

Some emissions from gas developments in the NT will need to be offset under a federal climate policy, the safeguard mechanism, that is applied to operations that emit more than 100,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. But that applies only to pollution directly from the facility, not the full lifecycle emissions as recommended by the Pepper inquiry.

King told the press club the safeguard mechanism would be applied to Beetaloo basin developments if emissions were above the threshold. “That is how we manage dealing with emissions in this country,” she said.
But research by Tim Baxter, of the consultancy Naru Research, found about 95% of emissions expected from four gas projects in the Beetaloo basin this decade would not have to be offset.
Baxter said King either “isn’t across her brief or she’s being intentionally misleading”.

“The Pepper inquiry was clear. For the territory to begin to manage the risks of fracking and unconventional gas in the NT all emissions occurring in Australia must be fully offset,” he said.
“The safeguard mechanism does not deliver this … If NT fracking is detonated, it could single-handedly undo all efforts to cut Australia’s climate emissions.”

Kirsty Howey, a former head of Environment Centre NT, now leading the Wilderness Society, said governments had broken a promise to fully act on the recommendations of the Pepper inquiry. “It’s one of the greatest failures of climate policy in history,” she said.

The acting chief head of Environment Centre NT, Bree Ahrens, called on the minister to “correct the public record”. She said an estimate by the energy company Santos suggested if the Beetaloo basin was fully developed and its gas burned it could lead to emissions 60 times what Australia releases into the atmosphere each year.
“Frackers are being given a free pass on climate emissions, and it’s the territory that will pay the price,” she said.

A spokesperson for King said successive NT governments had “accepted and implemented all 135 recommendations of the Pepper review”. They said the safeguard mechanism required all shale gas facilities, including Beetaloo basin gas extraction facilities, to have net zero emissions if they emitted more than 100,000 tonnes of CO2 a year.

articles.title: Queensland’s LNP has tread softly in government. It’s now baring its teeth over the power to break up workers’ strikes
articles.summary:
The controversial legislation may end up placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire

  • Get our

blocks.text: For almost two years, the Liberal National party’s strategy for government in Queensland has been to stay well clear of issues that risk burning through political capital.
On Wednesday, one of the most tentative conservative governments in recent history announced plans for sweeping and controversial changes to workplace laws.
In doing so, the LNP risks placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire.

The proposals would give the increasingly influential deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, the power to break strikes by public sector workers in certain circumstances, including if it is deemed “in the public interest”.

The government will also make it more difficult for public servants, including emergency services workers, to claim compensation for psychological injuries. Under the proposed laws, workers with such claims will only be entitled to support if they can show their workplace was the primary cause.

Law firm Slater and Gordon said the changes would make it harder for Queenslanders to access support for psychological injuries. The United Workers Union, which represents paramedics and some healthcare workers, said the changes were “an underhanded attack on Queensland ambulance officers and other hospital staff”.
Several business groups welcomed the changes.

The opposition leader, Steven Miles, said on Thursday morning the proposals were a “Newman-era attack on workers”, and the only thing surprising about that statement was that it took so long (roughly 14 hours) for the spectre of Campbell Newman’s government to, once again, loom over Queensland politics.

The collapse of the Newman government explains almost everything about the current one. The premier, David Crisafulli, and Bleijie had front-row seats for the “crash through” tactics that quickly turned voters off Newman, including proposals to sack public sector workers, and led to mass protests.

The lessons since have been that most suburban voters are uncomfortable with the LNP putting ideology on show. And so it went to the 2024 election – and won comfortably – talking mainly about crime and keeping all those vote-losing positions on things like abortion and budget cuts off the table.
Approaching the midway point of the term, the LNP has finally decided to show its teeth.
There are readers who will, understandably, take issue with the idea that the Crisafulli government has been “tentative” or has been, up to this point, unthreatening.
It has been unapologetic in attacking Indigenous representation within government, trans healthcare, and suppressing pro-Palestine protests.
These moves have been underpinned by a simple calculation: that the issues are marginal for most suburban and regional voters, whose concerns are mostly the cost of living and crime.

Those who care about evidence-based policy, human rights and civil liberties have every right to be furious. The polls suggest that fury hasn’t gone mainstream, and that suburban voters are OK with the government punching down, so long as it doesn’t affect them.
after newsletter promotion

Workplace reforms affect them. If nothing else, those survivors of the Newman government who still sit in the cabinet room will have learned a lesson that in Queensland, the public sector (which employs more than 320,000 people) is a powerful political bloc in its own right.
The morning after announcing the changes, Bleijie seemed only too aware of the scale of the coming fight.
“You’re going to see a mammoth campaign by the Labor party,” he told reporters at a press conference at Newstead.
“It’s going to be a lot of mistruths and misinformation, and I think everything they will be able to say … we will be able to debunk with facts.”

The Crisafulli government remains comfortably ahead in the relatively few public polls, a recent snapshot in Brisbane Times seemed to show Labor in Queensland had taken the biggest hit from the rise in support for One Nation.

But the bright orange cloud is still looming. And a simple look around the country reveals that in modern times, whether policy is decided by ideology or focus group, there’s no guarantee political capital will last.
Better use that capital while you can. Even if it means, as it will for the Queensland LNP, picking a fight with many of the suburban middle-class voters who put the party into office.

items: Ben Smee is Queensland state correspondent

articles.title: Palestine book co-written by Alana Hadid pulled from Random House just before release
articles.summary:
Hadid and Jenan Matari withdraw book planned for young readers after disputes with editors over characterizations of 7 October

A book on Palestine for young readers was pulled at Penguin…

blocks.text: A book on Palestine for young readers was pulled at Penguin Random House just before its scheduled release, following editorial disputes between the publisher and the book’s Palestinian American authors over their account of Palestinian history.

In November 2024, Random House Children’s Books, a division of Penguin Random House, signed the book deal with Alana Hadid, a philanthropist, activist and older sister of models Bella and Gigi, and Jenan Matari, an author and communications strategist. The book was promoted for release in September this year.

The authors, both influential social media commentators, drafted a manuscript about the history of Palestine, Israeli occupation, Palestinian resistance, and the diaspora, interwoven with references to their own families’ stories of displacement.

But the writers withdrew their book after objecting to edits by Random House that they said sanitized and misrepresented their views, and which they said were introduced after they thought the book had been finalized. A Random House spokesperson said the process “followed our standard bookmaking procedures”, and that the publisher ultimately supported the authors’ decision to pull the book.

Displacement and the Palestinian American Story would have been the eighth installment in Random House’s Race to the Truth series, an ongoing collection of nonfiction books for youth ages 10 to 13. The books aimed to provide the “true story of American history”, written by members of marginalized groups telling the histories of their peoples. A co-creator of the project said she objected to the treatment of Displacement and would not be pursuing future installments in the series with the publisher.

“It became clear that Penguin was never actually going to allow us just to write the book we wanted to write,” said Hadid. “It says a lot that they’re willing to tank an entire very powerful series that helps children learn history, just because of one book about Palestine.”

blocks.caption: Alana Hadid in 2025.  Photograph: Edward Berthelot/Getty Images

blocks.text: According to Hadid and Matari, who provided the Guardian with the draft manuscript and email excerpts of their communications with Random House, the authors and the publisher engaged in months of disagreements about language in the book, including a passage on the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks in southern Israel. The writers’ manuscript argued that people under “colonial domination” have the “right to resist”, but Random House urged them to incorporate arguments that the attacks that day violated international law. At an impasse, the authors withdrew their book in early September.
The authors now plan to release it through Interlink Books, a Palestinian-owned US publisher.

Random House Children’s Books has other forthcoming books on Palestine, the spokesperson said, writing: “We remain committed to bringing the Palestinian perspective to young readers.” The spokesperson also said another Race to the Truth book remained on track for 2028 publication.

The dispute over the book comes amid disproportionate scrutiny and censorship of work by and on behalf of Palestinians. The conflict also laid bare the wide gap between narratives around 7 October, one that could not be bridged in a book to be distributed by a mainstream publisher.

“I believe it was a revolutionary book, which is why it was under so much scrutiny,” Matari said. “They continued to try to sanitize our history because they didn’t want to make certain communities uncomfortable. But decolonial history is supposed to make you uncomfortable.”
‘No greater story to tell’

The Race to the Truth series was conceived by Saira Rao and Regina Jackson, founders of Race2Dinner, a program launched in 2019 to facilitate conversations with white women about racism. In 2020, Rao and Jackson sold a book called White Women to Penguin Random House, which became a bestseller, then in 2021 sold the Race to the Truth children’s series to the publishing house. Random House has since published books in the series on slavery, the colonization of the Wampanoag people, the exclusion of Chinese Americans, Mexican American history, and the forced assimilation of Indigenous youth.

blocks.caption: Jenan Matari. Photograph: Courtesy of Jenan Matari

blocks.text: As the series progressed, Rao felt it was urgent to publish a Palestine installment: “There’s no greater story to tell right now. Palestine actually tells a story of all genocides, of all settler colonial violence.”
After Random House greenlit the idea in summer of 2024, Rao brought on Matari and Hadid.

The authors submitted their first draft of Displacement in July 2025. In the introduction, they wrote that the Palestinian story had long been missing from classrooms. “The deliberate erasure of our history has left generations of Palestinians struggling to explain not only where we come from but why nearly half of us are scattered around the world, including – as in our cases – in the United States,” the intro said.

The book discussed the landscape and history of Palestine; the rise of Zionism; the Nakba, or catastrophe, of 1948 when more than 700,000 Palestinian people were expelled from their homes; their analysis of Israel as a “settler colony”; the relationship between the US and Israel; and life for Palestinians living under military occupation.

They also documented their family histories. Hadid’s grandparents, they wrote, were expelled from Safed days after her father was born, becoming refugees in Syria. And relatives of Matari and her husband were displaced from Deir Yassin and Ein Karem after an April 1948 massacre claimed the lives of more than 100 Palestinians.
“I just wanted children to see us as humans,” Hadid said.
Disputes about 7 October

Tensions arose on the project in June 2026 when, according to the authors, the book was distributed to reviewers and made available for preorder before Random House had shared a final version with the writers. When the authors received a copy, they said it included changes to a passage about 7 October made by Random House without their knowledge.

In a chapter called The International Right to Armed Resistance, the authors cited a UN general assembly resolution that said people under colonial domination are entitled to “the right to self-determination” and to restore that right “by any means at their disposal”. The chapter also noted Hamas’s use of prisoner exchanges to free thousands of Palestinians imprisoned in Israel they called “effectively hostages of the state”. Referring to the 2011 exchange of captured Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit for more than 1,000 prisoners, they wrote: “This exchange was one of the most famous and showed Palestinians that resistance could bring real results.”

On 7 October, the manuscript continued, Hamas fighters “crossed into Israel in a coordinated assault”. The authors said roughly 1,100 Israelis were killed, including 37 children, and said civilians and soldiers were taken captive “to be used in an exchange”.

Their section on 7 October was brief, but argued that international law authorized Palestinian resistance “by any means necessary”, saying the attacks came after “decades of ignored suffering and repression”.

“Palestinians, like other oppressed peoples before them, have demanded freedom in the face of overwhelming military power. What happened on October 7 was not the beginning of violence in this land – it was another moment in a long history of a people struggling to be free,” they wrote.

The authors said they had, at Random House’s request, added details about the 7 October death toll, and they believed the language was finalized in May 2026. However, when they received an updated final copy of the book, they saw that a Random House editor had added a line about the 7 October attacks saying: “These actions were a violation of international law.”

The authors objected to the insertion, emails show, saying it contradicted their analysis of international law. They claimed in an email it was also a violation of their contract to make changes without their approval. One Random House editor suggested in an email that without that line or something similar, “we will lose all credibility with our readers, including those who are open-minded about our perspective” and the book couldn’t be published.

Back-and-forth negotiations surrounding the description of 7 October continued for weeks, emails show, with Random House’s head of publicity, legal department and children’s books president involved in discussions.

In the meantime, Random House came back with other edits the authors found objectionable. In July, a senior Random House official suggested removing “Jewish” as a modifier in several places, including when the authors had referred to Zionist militias involved in the destruction of Palestinian villages during the Nakba as “Jewish gangs”. “Our concern is not accuracy, but whether the repetition adds necessary clarity,” the Random House official wrote.

The authors responded that it was “shameful” for an editor to say accuracy was not the concern, prompting an editor to reply back: “Our editorial point was not about whether the word was accurate, but whether, given the context, repeating the [Jewish] modifier was necessary.”

A Random House official again pressed the authors to expand on 7 October, writing in an email that the authors could add context along the lines of: “Some human rights organizations and commentators have described Hamas’s actions that day as violations of international law; others frame the legal and historical questions differently.”

But the authors grew increasingly frustrated, writing in one email: “In a book about the history of slavery in the United States – neither of us can imagine a Black author being forced to condemn the slave rebellions or consider them a violation of international law.”
In one email to their agent, Matari wrote, “It has become quite clear that Penguin is more focused and concerned with centering Jewish feelings over Palestinian life and lived experience.”

Records show Random House repeatedly expressed their commitment to the book, with one official saying they were dedicated to publishing “a necessary and accessible book about the Palestinian American story for young readers, a perspective that remains far too rare in children’s nonfiction” and saying editors wanted to work in “good faith” to resolve issues.

By August, Random House suggested adding a “publisher’s note” to the book with some of the suggested 7 October language and changing the age range to 14+, but also said if the parties could not resolve their differences, the authors could take the book elsewhere and keep their advance.

“Editorial discussion and revision are a standard part of the publishing process,” the Random House spokesperson said in an email. “We gave guidance to help ensure the intended readers for this book, ages 10 and up, had enough information to understand the subject matter and engage thoughtfully with the questions it raises, knowing that many readers would be coming to the subject matter for the first time.”

The spokesperson said the company had made digital advance copies available to industry contacts, which were marked as “uncorrected” and not final, and that this process was halted after the authors expressed concerns. “We would not move forward with a book that the authors were not comfortable publishing,” the spokesperson said.
‘No longer the book we wrote’

In an interview, Matari said she felt it was unacceptable for Random House to publish a disclaimer that might contradict their writing. Termination, she said, seemed the only option: “It was no longer the book we wrote.”

Matari was no stranger to backlash for her commentary on 7 October. Over the last year, several scheduled book talks for her debut children’s book, about a young Palestinian girl and her grandfather, were cancelled last-minute after people accused her of antisemitism, in part over social media posts describing the 7 October attacks as resistance against colonialism and declaring the US to be “under Zionist occupation”. She and a Jewish author recently sued the city of Los Angeles for free speech violations after the public library cancelled their planned joint book event. Matari has denied claims of antisemitism and defended her posts, saying she was “vehemently anti-Zionist”.

blocks.caption: Saira Rao. Photograph: Rebecca Stumpf/The Guardian

blocks.text: Hadid said they were not trying to minimize the harms of 7 October and had, at Random House’s request, been clear about the death toll. Their goal was to put the attacks into historical context. “I wasn’t going to publish this book with words I hadn’t written, where they were forcing us to tell the story from the perspective of the oppressors.”

Rao, from the Race to the Truth series, said her relationship with Random House had been smooth before the conflicts over the Palestine book, with previous authors given significant leeway to write their stories without interference. Hadid and Matari’s experience was fundamentally different, Rao said: “You’ve got the entire company weighing in on this one little book.”

The end of the series at Random House comes at a time when a wide range of industries and institutions are backtracking on diversity, equity and inclusion efforts, raising fears about diminishing opportunities for people of color in academia, publishing, entertainment and media. The recent rise of book bans and open hostility to diverse works is further diminishing those opportunities, said Leyla Moushabeck, co-owner and longtime editor at Interlink, the publishing house taking on Hadid and Matari’s book.
“As a second-generation Palestinian-American, it’s a book I wish I had had growing up,” Moushabeck said of the book, which Interlink plans to publish next year.
Hadid added she was grateful their manuscript found a new home: “We hope that people read the book that Penguin didn’t want you to read.”

articles.title: Fisheries minister travelling to China ahead of lobster, crab tariff deadline
articles.summary: Canada's fisheries minister will be travelling to China at the end of the month, ahead of a looming tariff deadline affecting the lobster and crab industries.

image.caption: Minister of Fisheries Joanne Thompson will travel to China later this month, where she will push to improve market access for Canadian fish and seafood, according to a spokesperson. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Canada's fisheries minister will be travelling to China at the end of the month, ahead of a looming tariff deadline affecting the lobster and crab industries.
Market access for Canadian fish, seafood and deepening trade relations are key priorities, spokesperson says
As part of an agreement in January, China suspended a 25 per cent tariff on Canadian lobster and crab until the end of the year.
It's still not clear whether the suspension will be extended, leaving the lobster and crab industries uncertain if they will soon have reduced access to a major seafood market.
Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson is planning a trip to China to discuss this and other key topics, her office confirmed on Thursday.

In a statement, a spokesperson said the minister aims to "deepen trade relationships with her counterparts, discuss market access for Canadian fish and seafood products and continue supporting Canadian harvesters and industry to get more seafood to market around the world."
The duties impact about 80 per cent of Canadian seafood exports to China and were imposed in 2025, after Ottawa slapped tariffs on Chinese steel, aluminum and electric vehicles.

items: Finance minister leaves China with pork tariffs still in place
Some Canadians in Beijing say now is time to do business in China

blocks.text: According to Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) trade data, crab and lobster make up the majority of Canada's fish and seafood exports to China.
Federal figures show that $1.3 billion in Canadian seafood exports went to China in 2024.

"China is Canada's second-largest seafood export partner, and predictable market access is imperative to the future success of Canada's fish and seafood industry," said a spokesperson for Thompson in a statement.
"We are growing our trading partnerships and building up Canadian industry to diversify into new markets."
On Thursday, Thompson is expected to make an announcement in Moncton, N.B., alongside her Atlantic Canadian counterparts.

In January, China agreed to lower tariffs on canola seed and suspend them on seafood and some agricultural products, in exchange for Canada allowing the import of 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles per year at a much lower tariff rate.
According DFO, Canada exported $8.5 billion in fish and seafood to 114 countries last year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: Bärbel Bas' resignation shows harsh tone of German politics
articles.summary: Germany's Labor Minister Bärbel Bas has stepped down, citing a family bereavement and the harsh realities of political life. Why is German politics today so often unforgiving?

image.caption: Bas (right) stepped down following criticism from Merz (left)Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: For a brief moment, a sense of quiet sympathy could be felt in Berlin's often unforgiving political arena: On Monday morning, federal labor minister and co-leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) Bärbel Bas announced her resignation from all government and party positions. The 58-year-old politician cited a personal tragedy as the reason for her decision: "Following the death of my stepdaughter, I have come to realize that I need time to work through my grief," Bas wrote in a statement.

Bas also said that sustained criticism from the center-right conservative parties, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU), had contributed to her decision to step down. In her statement, she wrote that she had been forced to "conclude that public attacks on me, unfortunately also from within the ranks of our coalition partner, continued to intensify during this personally difficult time."
Merz reportedly criticized Bas in an off-the-record briefing

Bas had recently been responsible for implementing complex reforms to Germany's public pension system and had been urged by some conservative politicians, in rather harsh terms, not to delay the project any further.

According to a report in the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, one remark in particular appears to have weighed heavily on her: A comment allegedly made by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, of the CDU, during an off-the-record briefing with journalists.

Was this, then, a politician who felt so overwhelmed by pressure, both personal and political, that she chose to step down rather than continue to endure it? Berlin-based political and media scholar Mirco Liefke has long studied the dynamics of public communication.

He told DW that unfairness and harshness have always been part of politics, but added: "What I do think is new is the potential for escalation and the speed that social media have brought to public debate. Along with that has come an incentive for individual actors to adopt ever more radical positions."

blocks.caption: Bas was in charge of implementing a crucial pension reformImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Politics and the media: What goes public, what stays hidden?

Emotions and speed are the driving forces, while social media amplifies both these. Another consequence is that there are hardly any spaces left where politicians can speak in confidence. Merz is said to have made critical remarks of Bas during an off-the-record briefing whose contents were not intended for publication.
He reportedly remarked that Bas was barely visible in public and failing to put forward proposals of her own, though the chancellor was aware of the SPD leader's personal circumstances.

A spokesperson for Merz declined to confirm or deny the account, but by then the remarks had long since entered the public domain. As Liefke puts it: "It has effectively become a business model to leak information that is meant to remain confidential and thereby generate attention."
Green Party co-leader Banaszak: 'No backing from the SPD'

The co-leader of Germany's center-left Green Party, Felix Banaszak, comes from the same city as Bas, Duisburg, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, and has known the former SPD leader for many years.
"Toughness and ruthlessness are nothing new in politics," he told DW. "But we still need to find a different way of doing things if we do not want to keep wearing people down."

Banaszak also holds his colleagues in the SPD accountable: "The fact that Bärbel Bas encountered so little understanding for her personal situation from within the ranks of the coalition partner, and that apparently no one in the SPD was willing to step forward, defend her, and take her out of the line of fire, is simply not a good sign."
"It would be naive to pretend that the attacks on a man would have unfolded in a similar way," Banaszak added.
Liefke agrees: "Women politicians are subjected to an extraordinary degree of misogynistic and sexualized abuse, and they face a level of public exposure that is entirely new."
CDU pushes back

The debate over how Bas and her grief should have been treated soon took on some of the same characteristics as the attacks that had preceded her resignation. Manuela Schwesig, SPD premier of the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, described the attacks by the CDU/CSU as "inhuman," drawing sharp criticism from many conservative politicians. Merz, meanwhile, publicly expressed his regret over Bas' resignation, and wished her all the best.

For Liefke, this is simply another facet of the growing emotionalization of politics. Once a politician decides to step down, he argues, public expressions of concern are often far more intense than they used to be and come from all sides: "This is a facade of concern," he said. "There is something ritualistic, almost reflexive, about it. People react this way because they are following another major trend: Emotionalization."

blocks.caption: SPD General Secretary Kevin Kühnert resigned citing constant threats from far-right extremistsImage: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The case of Kevin Kühnert

The attacks on Bas are just one example of the increasingly harsh tone of political debate. Formal reprimands in the Bundestag have risen sharply, particularly since the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) entered parliament in 2017. High-profile resignations have also made headlines, including that of Kevin Kühnert, the SPD's former secretary-general.

Kühnert stepped down in 2024, citing health reasons. In April 2025, however, he told Die Zeit newspaper that he had felt constantly threatened by far-right extremists. Political debate, he said, is showing "an increasing lack of respect for the views of those who think differently."

blocks.caption: Helmut Schmidt managed to maintain his private life throughout his chancellorshipImage: picture alliance / ASSOCIATED PRESS

blocks.text: Former Chancellor Helmut Schmidt: A public figure, yet still private

Liefke points out that politicians once managed to maintain two distinct modes of communication: One public and one private. "When you think of earlier generations of politicians, what comes to mind is the distance they maintained, the relative lack of emotional display. Take Helmut Schmidt, for example. He did not openly grieve over things that came crashing down on him. At least, he did not show it publicly." Helmut Schmidt, of the SPD, served as chancellor from 1974 to 1982.

Liefke argues: "Today, politicians such as Bärbel Bas benefit from drawing on their own life stories when they say, 'I come from a working-class background and worked my way up.' That can work to their advantage, but it also makes them far more visible, and far more vulnerable, as individuals."

Bas, who served as president of the Bundestag from 2021 to 2025, intends to retain her parliamentary seat. Life is likely to become quieter for her now, while others move into the spotlight, both in public and, perhaps, in private as well.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Russell Brand told woman ‘it’s just fun’ as he raped her, court hears
articles.summary:
Southwark crown court jury is shown video of woman telling detectives about alleged attack in 1999

A woman has alleged Russell Brand told her “it’s just fun” as he raped her in a hotel room…

blocks.text: A woman has alleged Russell Brand told her “it’s just fun” as he raped her in a hotel room at the 1999 Labour party conference, a court has heard.
The alleged victim told detectives the comedian made her feel sick and dirty as he assaulted her despite her pleading: “Get off me, please stop. It hurts.”

Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.
The 51-year-old fixed his gaze on one of the TV screens at Southwark crown court on Thursday as a video of the woman’s interview from 27 September 2023 was played.

She told police she met Brand at a fringe cabaret event that he was performing in during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. She was not attracted to the then unknown performer, whom she assumed was gay and showered her with compliments.
But she found him polite and intelligent, and the pair spoke about their work before going back to her hotel room to continue their conversation.

The woman said she “froze” in the run-down single room when she returned from the toilet to find that Brand was partly naked and “prancing around” like an ostrich. He also asked her to take photographs of him. She said she asked him why he had undressed, and he told her: “Don’t worry, I’m mostly naked at home.”
She told police he then raped her in an attack that lasted up to 10 minutes and left her feeling frightened, in pain, and like she couldn’t breathe.
“He did rape, he did push me on the bed,” she told police. “He did pull my clothes off, he took my trousers off.

“I remember him on me, very heavy. I know I said no. I kind of drifted out of my head. I couldn’t get out of the situation – ‘do I shout, do I scream?’ He was very heavy, I couldn’t breathe, it didn’t take long.”
She described his body as snake-like and “disgusting” and said his tongue was “horrible” like a lizard.

“I’m saying ‘no, no’ but I was really scared. I know he groped me. I know he was touching me, I know he grabbed my breasts. I know he tried to kiss me and I moved my neck. I didn’t want his mouth on mine,” she told police.
“He was just pulling my trousers down and pulling my underwear off, and he was inside me. It was not nice, it was painful and it hurt.”

She said she closed her eyes during the attack and hoped it would be over quickly. She recalled: “He was making noises, a lot of noises of enjoyment and saying how pretty I was. I remember him complimenting me, saying: ‘Are you enjoying it’? I remember him asking me. Obviously I didn’t answer.”
She alleged that Brand spoke as the attack was unfolding. She told police: “He was just saying: ‘We’re having fun, it’s fine, it’s all good, don’t worry about it, it’s just fun, it’s normal.’”
The woman, who had been a victim of abuse in the past, said Brand made her compare earlier experiences, and it “stuck in her head … is this what abusers do?”
She told police: “It was almost like to convince me it’s all OK and that I’d enjoy it, that I’d have to learn to enjoy it.”
In the aftermath, she said Brand acted “like nothing was wrong”, wrote down his email address, and suggested that his mother might like to meet her.

The following morning, she banged her head against the wall because she felt numb. She told police she had had nightmares about being pregnant and said she kept quiet about the incident for years as she watched Brand becoming “more and more famous”.
The woman said a 2023 Dispatches documentary about allegation of sexual misconduct by Brand “triggered” her to go to police.
Brand denies the allegations. The trial continues.

articles.title: Hamburg court jails 2 men over plot to attack Jewish leaders on behalf of Iran
articles.summary: The pair was found guilty of espionage and attempted murder. The court says they planned to attack the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany and president of the German-Israeli society.

image.caption: The men were sentenced in Hamburg after being extradited from Denmark [FILE: October 3, 2020]Image: xim.gs/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced two men accused of plotting to target Jewish leaders in Germany on behalf of Iran'ssecret service to multiple years in prison.

Both were found guilty of espionage and attempted murder. One defendant was given a four-and-a-half year sentence, while the other received an eight-and-a-half year sentence as the mastermind of the planned attacks.
Prosecutors said that one defendant, a 54-year-old Dane with Afghan roots, had received his orders directly from Iran's al-Quds Brigades, the foreign arm of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.
The man was said to have recruited his accomplice, a 43-year-old Afghan man living in Denmark, to carry out one of the attacks, or find someone who could.
The 43-year-old was also tasked with finding a weapon with which to carry out one of the attacks.
Beyond targeting two high-profile individuals, the 54-year-old had reportedly made preparations for an arson attack on a kosher deli in Berlin.
The defendants were arrested by Danish authorities in the city of Aarhus last year and extradited to Germany.
How Europe, the US can better protect Jewish communities
Who were convicted defendants planning to attack?
Among the figures the pair planned to attack was Josef Schuster, the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, the court found.
Another prospective target was Green Party politician Volker Beck, president of the German-Israeli society.
Beck called on Berlin to expel Iran's ambassador and consular officials after charges against the men were made public.
"Jewish life and a commitment to the Jewish and democratic state are repeatedly threatened with murder and attacked by the regime of the Islamic Republic of Iran on German soil," he said.

Germany's Foreign Office summoned Iran's ambassador after Danish authorities made the arrests, prompting the Iranian embassy in Berlin to release a statement rejecting what it called "unfounded allegations made at the behest of Iran's enemies."

articles.title: DSWD urges content creators to be respectful of PWDs
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) told content creators to be more respectful of people with mental health conditions.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 9:37pm

Every individual with a disability, including those on the autism spectrum or with neurodevelopmental conditions, deserves dignity, respect, privacy, and the utmost care, DSWD said. (Photo from DSWD FB post)
The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) told content creators to be more respectful of people with mental health conditions.
The agency issued the statement in response to a viral incident wherein the hosts of the podcast Machong Chismisan made fun of people on the autism spectrum.

"Every individual with a disability, including those on the autism spectrum or with neurodevelopmental conditions, deserves dignity, respect, privacy, and the utmost care. Exploiting a person's disability for amusement, ridicule, or online engagement is unacceptable, as it reinforces harmful stereotypes and drives discrimination against a vulnerable group," DSWD spokesperson Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao said.

"We urge all content creators to exercise responsibility in discussing topics that make fun and violate the rights of vulnerable sectors such as persons with disabilities, whether it is apparent or non-apparent. We need to protect their dignity not only as an act of compassion but also as part of upholding their human rights," she added.
Dumlao said that content creators have the responsibility of fostering inclusive digital spaces and ensuring that they are mindful of the rights of vulnerable people.
The DSWD said that under the Magna Carta for Persons with Disabilities, any act that shames, ridicules, or vilifies a person with disabilities is punishable under the law.
While the agency did not name names, the controversial episode of Machong Chismisan poked fun at Josh Aquino, the son of media personality Kris Aquino.
The hosts of the show have since apologized and taken down the episode following the backlash. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account
articles.summary:
Move comes as Senator Elizabeth Warren condemns Barclays response to questions over ex-boss’s ties to sex offender

US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s…

blocks.text: US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.

It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.

A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.

The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department.

Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”

News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executives Jes Staley and his links to Epstein.

Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American banker resigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan.

blocks.caption: A FCA investigation concluded that Jes Staley and Jeffrey Epstein had a relationship that ‘went beyond one that was professional in nature’. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

blocks.text: The Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were “indeed close” and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”.

Staley was eventually banned from the UK’s financial sector in 2023 for playing down those ties, and failed to overturn that decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year.

That included Staley admitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staff in New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchange referring to Disney princesses, in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing.
After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”.

In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: In July, Elizabeth Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair asking how it had vetted its former chief executive. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

blocks.text: Barclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient.

The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”.

“This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”.

Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.”
Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.

articles.title: ‘No person is walang kwenta’: Groups, friends defend Josh Aquino amid podcast controversy
articles.summary: The NBI is set to probe the hosts of the 'Machong Chismisan' podcast following public backlash over offensive remarks mocking Josh Aquino

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Podcasts have given ordinary people a platform to speak their minds. Some give us a chance at self-reflection, while others offer comedic relief.
But what happens when the jokes being thrown around in the latter begin to draw more offense than laughter?
In a Machong Chismisan podcast episode published on October 5, Kris Aquino’s son Josh became the subject of mockery as the show’s host, Tito P, referred to him as “walang kwenta (useless).”

While the controversial episode has already been taken down, the Machong Chismisan podcast was not spared from public scrutiny, with groups and newsmakers attesting that the hosts had crossed the line with their remarks.

National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) director Melvin Matibag also confirmed to Boy Abunda in a text message on Thursday, October 15, that he has ordered the NBI’s cybercrime division and special action unit to probe the podcast’s hosts and file the necessary complaints.
The Machong Chismisan podcast’s contract has also been terminated by The Pod Network “effective immediately.”

Figures who know Josh personally were quick to come to his defense — with Abunda expressing outrage over the incident on an episode of Fast Talk With Boy Abunda. The talk show host said he was puzzled that a group of men who appeared to be intelligent and educated could make such cruel remarks about another young man with a disability.
Abunda recalled that when Josh’s mother, Kris Aquino, was actively seeking treatment in the US, it was his job to gather everyone each morning for a prayer.

“Hindi po walang silbi si Josh. Mali po ang inyong ginawa. Labag sa batas ng Diyos at sa batas ng tao ang inyong ginawa. Napakasakit. Napakasakit, hindi lamang para sa pamilya, pero para sa lahat ng mga pamilya, ng mga bata, ng mga magulang na may kapansanan, na may disability ang kanilang mga anak,” Abunda emphasized.

(Josh is not useless. What you did was wrong. What you did is against the teachings of God and the law. It hurts. It hurts, not just for Josh’s family, but for all the families, children, and parents of those with disabilities.)
Abunda recommended that Kris press charges against the podcast — citing RA 7277, or the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, which penalizes those who publicly ridicule persons with disabilities.

“Labag sa batas ang ginawa ng mga podcasters na ito. Congratulations, you got the attention of everybody, at hindi dito nagtatapos. Dapat ito’y pag-aralan, dapat tayo’y magreact. Dapat pag-usapan, para maenlighten ang maraming tao. I am sorry for what happened to Josh,” Abunda added.

(What these podcasters did is against the law. Congratulations, you got the attention of everybody, and it doesn’t end here. This should be studied, and we should react. It should be talked about, so we can enlighten even more people. I am sorry for what happened to Josh.)
Meanwhile, Mark Leviste, who was previously in a relationship with Kris, stepped in to publicly defend Josh.

“I love him like my own son, and my children love him like their own older brother. He is one of the kindest, sweetest, most prayerful, and loving people you will ever meet. Sinuman ang tunay na nakakakilala sa kanya ay mauunawaan kung bakit labis na nakasasakit sa aming mga nagmamahal sa kanya ang mga binitiwang salita tungkol sa kanya,”
(Those who truly know Josh understand why it hurts to hear these words be thrown against him.)
Leviste asked that the people behind Machong Chismisan take full responsibility for what transpired, personally apologize to Josh and his family, and ensure that the incident does not happen again.

“You may call yourselves comedians or podcasters, but freedom of expression does not exempt you from accountability! There’s a difference between making people laugh and turning someone into a laughingstock. When your foolish words and slapstick humor demean someone, especially because of his disability, you cross a line that should never be crossed!” Leviste wrote.
Designer Michael Leyva, a longtime friend of Kris, also came to Josh’s defense — personally vouching for Josh’s kindness.
“Making Kuya Josh the subject of your so-called ‘Machong Chismisan’ podcast and mocking his disability is not something that I or any of us should simply let slide,” he said in an Instagram story.

Even the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) had to issue a warning for content creators to be careful about making derogatory statements towards individuals with mental disabilities not just as an act of compassion, but to uphold their human rights.
And for the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA), it no longer becomes comedy when one’s dignity is involved, but instead, it is “blatant discrimination.”

“Creators bear a responsibility to foster respectful and inclusive digital spaces, ensuring that all content is approached with sensitivity and mindfulness. NCDA also calls on the public and social media users to refrain from sharing, reposting, and engaging with any material that demeans, mocks, or exploits vulnerable individuals,” the NCDA wrote.
In the same vein, the Council for the Welfare of Children reminded content creators and media practitioners of the influence they hold over shaping public opinion.

The Down Syndrome Association of the Philippines encouraged Machong Chismisan’s hosts — and in effect, all content creators — to engage with individuals with autism, Down syndrome, and other disabilities for them to hear their stories and use their platforms “to build understanding rather than ridicule.”

“No person is walang kwenta (useless). Every person with autism, Down syndrome, or any disability has inherent dignity and worth. Using their condition as a punchline is not comedy. It is cruelty that hurts thousands of Filipino families who live this reality every day,” the group wrote in its statement.
The Autism Society of the Philippines also advised against patronizing content creators and podcasts “not capable of basic respect.”
“Freedom of expression must never come at the expense of the rights and humanity of persons with disabilities,” the group said.

articles.title: AI-assisted euthanasia? New film addresses prospect of care robots
articles.summary: While the world debates the dangers of artificial intelligence, filmmaker Doris Dörrie explores how humanoid robots could change the way we deal with aging, caregiving and how people choose to die.

image.caption: A care robot named Pavlovich takes over the care of Mrs. WinklerImage: Mathias Bothor/Zeitsprung Pictures/Wild Bunch Germany/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hamburg in the near future: Instead of delivery drivers, robots deliver parcels. In cafés, talking and serving robots roll between the tables. On the streets, one encounters humanoid robots walking dogs — or the other way around, people taking their robot dogs for a walk.

This is the setting of Doris Dörrie's new film, "Frau Winkler verlässt das Haus" ("Mrs. Winkler Leaves the House"). At the core of the plot is an elderly woman who can no longer live on her own after a fall. With her only daughter unable to provide permanent care, the solution seems simple enough: a care robot with a built-in EOL program, or "End of Life" mode. This robot not only assists with everyday life but can also provide assisted dying under certain conditions, namely when the person explicitly wishes to end their life and meets the relevant medical criteria.

Dörrie's film tackles several major social issues with remarkable lightness. These include the challenges facing ageing societies such as Germany, Japan and China, the question of dying on one's own terms and a mother-daughter relationship that raises questions of guilt and responsibility. Even though the story is set in Germany, such issues resonate globally.
"I write about what personally moves and interests me," Dörrie tells DW.

One of the best-known contemporary German film directors, Doris Dörrie achieved her breakthrough in 1985 with the comedy "Men…," and later gained international recognition with films such as "Cherry Blossoms" and "Greetings from Fukushima."
Who decides when we die?

Assisted suicide is one of the most complex ethical questions of our time. Laws vary considerably around the world. While some countries permit active euthanasia under certain conditions, others prohibit and criminalize all forms of assisted suicide.
What is assisted suicide and where does Germany stand?
In her film, Doris Dörrie asks what happens when AI begins calculating the cost of caring for an elderly person and weighing whether that cost is still "worth" bearing for society.

But the underlying idea isn't new, Dörrie says, pointing to the Japanese legend of Narayama, which is also mentioned in the film. According to the legend, the eldest children were responsible for taking their ageing parents to a mountain and leaving them there to die because there was not enough food for everyone. "And that's also the debate we are currently facing to a certain extent: Can we really afford to let older people live longer and longer?"

In Dörrie's film, elderly people are allowed to make their own decisions once they reach a certain state of health, but they can't change their minds afterwards. Yet what does it really mean to make a decision freely? "It's a tricky situation," says Dörrie, because the question is to what extent one is also pressured into making this decision, "not only because it makes more economic sense, but also because one is no longer a burden on one's loved ones — in this case, one's daughter..."

The film often raises these questions indirectly and with plenty of dark humor. At one point, a care adviser presents the EOL feature to Mrs. Winkler as an attractive and, above all, straightforward additional option, making it sound as though there would be nothing more for her to worry about.

blocks.caption: Doris Dörrie (left) with actors Angela Winkler and Laura TonkeImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Staying close despite the algorithm

Dörrie is not interested in demonizing AI in her film — quite the opposite. In the film, the care robot, which Mrs. Winkler names Pavlovich, helps the elderly woman rediscover some of her zest for life and get out of the house.

"When you travel through Germany, you see small houses everywhere," Dörrie says, "and statistics show that an elderly person lives alone in every other house. If AI can help in these circumstances, why not use it?" The filmmaker says it's precisely this ambiguity she wants to explore in her film. Dividing things into black and white would neither be interesting nor, in her view, accurate.

Dörrie and her film crew were also surprised during filming by how quickly people can develop an emotional bond with a robot. She attributes this to the human brain. "We regard anything that moves and speaks as a living being. We can't help it," she explains. And that is precisely what we need to pay attention to when interacting with AI, Dörrie says. "How often are we truly aware that we are talking to a machine rather than a living being? These are things we still have to learn."
How robots are helping solve China's elderly care crisis
The difference between humans and machines

Looking at the development of AI, it seems that the boundaries between humans and machines are becoming increasingly blurred. That is precisely why we need to talk about it, Doris Dörrie says. In her view, things become problematic "when we can no longer distance ourselves from technology and stop forming our own thoughts."

As human beings, we need to ask ourselves who we are and what truly defines us, Dörrie says. "I believe there is a major difference between robots and us, and that is the ability to play. A robot might be able to initiate a game, she explains, "but play itself is something profoundly human because it has no particular meaning or purpose."

Alongside these philosophical questions about what it means to be human, the filmmaker also makes a clear call for AI regulation: "At some point, we had to discuss nuclear weapons internationally, too. We've talked about all kinds of issues in the past, and we haven't just talked about them — we've also managed to find solutions," she points out.
She says this is something that urgently needs to be addressed. "And I believe we need to move very quickly on this, too."
This article was originally written in German.
