articles.title: DOJ: Philippines has yet to criminalize foreign interference
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday said the Philippines has yet to enact a law specifically defining and criminalizing foreign interference, pointing to gaps in existing espionage laws.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 9:01pm
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday said the Philippines has yet to enact a law specifically defining and criminalizing foreign interference, pointing to gaps in existing espionage laws.

During a Senate Committee on National Defense and Security, Peace, Unification and Reconciliation hearing on several bills concerning espionage, Senator Erwin Tulfo asked security agencies how they define threats to national security.

“We have not yet in our existing laws actually defined and criminalized foreign interference. We already have an established crime which is espionage. It's just a matter of Mr. Chair, of modernizing our definition of espionage,” DOJ Senior State Counsel Fretti Ganchoon said.

“Espionage is an established crime already, but with respect to foreign interference, we have not yet criminalized it. And so, if ever, this is going to be the first time that the Philippines will criminalize foreign interference,” she added.

Ganchoon cited a 2025 incident in which Chinese nationals were charged with espionage after they were arrested with equipment suspected of being used for spying. She added that the matter had not reached the DOJ.

She said the incident highlighted potential gaps in existing laws, particularly in cases involving the possession of suspected espionage equipment without the actual acquisition of classified information.

“Because indeed there are gaps in our laws… Perhaps it would be difficult if there's no actual obtention or getting of classified information in such a case and it's just mere possession of this equipment, Mr. Chair,” Ganchoon said.

Meanwhile, former National Security Council assistant director general Jonathan Malaya also said existing espionage laws were inadequate to cover certain acts involving sensitive government information.

“So, if an act of espionage is not committed against military installations—for example, [if it involves] secrets of the Department of Foreign Affairs, the Office of the President, or other civilian government agencies—that would not be covered by Commonwealth Act No. 616 or Article 117 of the Revised Penal Code,” Malaya said.
Enacted in 1941, when the Philippines was under US rule, Commonwealth Act No. 616 penalizes espionage and certain disloyal acts affecting the Philippines and the United States. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Bring a bottle: Viennese dog owners told to dilute their pets’ urine to protect trees
articles.summary:
Officials issue guidance saying the ammonia in animal urine should be watered down to stop it corroding bark

A neighbourhood in Vienna has introduced guidelines for dog walking, including…

blocks.text: A neighbourhood in Vienna has introduced guidelines for dog walking, including the use of bottled tap water to rinse away urine and protect vulnerable trees.
Neubau, an up-and-coming, densely populated district dotted with cafes and galleries, rolled out the Schönes Gassi (nice dog walk) campaign this week.
The project addresses the impact of the area’s 600 dogs on greenery, including about 250 trees planted over the past decade to help mitigate the effects of the climate crisis.

Using the slogan Das Flascherl zum Sackerl (the bottle to go with the bag), the guidelines say animal urine corrodes tree bark, weakening its protective layer and potentially letting corrosive pathogens and fungi penetrate the trunk.

“While marking territory is a form of communication for dogs, it causes stress for urban trees,” said Grätzllabor, a community group that takes its name from the Viennese slang for quarter or neighbourhood. “This results in rot and, in the worst case, compromised stability.”
The group said the campaign had been launched in concert with “concerned citizens” in the Austrian capital. It also asks owners to carry plastic bags to clean up after their pets.
Owners can pick up a free 270ml water bottle at the town hall to rinse areas used by their dogs. The voluntary scheme could be expanded to other districts.
Fresh canine urine is highly water-soluble and dilution significantly reduces the concentration of ammonia and other harmful substances seeping into the soil, while also softening the smell.
Grätzllabor said the rinsing strategy should not be interpreted as a “licence” for dogs to mark trees or green space but rather as an action owners could take to minimise harm caused by their pets.
Conny Sporrer, who is a dog trainer, said the Schönes Gassi campaign could help head off more drastic calls to mitigate problems linked to animal waste.

“In Vienna, we don’t need a city full of dog bans, or a city where dogs are just allowed to urinate anywhere they please,” she told reporters, saying most pets could be taught where to relieve themselves. “What we need is consideration, education and sufficient suitable facilities for dogs.”
after newsletter promotion

Similar schemes have been introduced in Japan, Italy, Switzerland and Spain, which has the highest share of dog-owning households in the EU at 70%. Austria has relatively low levels of ownership, at just 17% of households.

Berlin, where more than 100,000 dogs are kept as pets after a surge in ownership during the pandemic, has also begun addressing the problem by stopping the planting of black locust trees in some areas because they are particularly sensitive to urine.
In the spring, the western district of Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf began installing “pee stones” for dogs to use as a target, instead of trees.

articles.title: ‘Fantastically special’: all 10 Victoria Crosses awarded to Royal Marines go on show for first time
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Portsmouth Historic Dockyard’s new £15m permanent display tells tales of courage from conflicts such as Crimean and both world wars

They tell tales of bravery under fire, may lead…

blocks.text: They tell tales of bravery under fire, may lead to conversations about the UK’s place in the world and could prompt visitors to reflect on what they might have done if faced with the same perilous circumstances.

All 10 Victoria Crosses (VCs) awarded to members of the Royal Marines are going on display together for the first time along with tales of courage during conflicts such as the Crimean and both world wars.

“It’s fantastically special,” said Matthew Sheldon, the chief executive officer of Royal Navy Museums. “The Royal Marines have only ever been awarded 10 Victoria Crosses. We have all 10 of them. The originals have never been seen together before. They’ve been in secure storage, not visible to the public, which seemed like a crying shame.”
The medals will go on permanent display at a new £15m “Royal Marines Experience” at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard telling 360 years of marines’ history.

Sheldon said the marines awarded VCs tended to be “youngish” and not from very senior ranks. Like modern marines, who usually work in small, agile teams, they tended to find themselves in very close quarters to the enemy.
He said the stories could lead to debate about the role the UK played in global conflicts.

blocks.caption: Mark Berry, the assistant curator of artefacts at Royal Navy Museums, installing the Victoria Crosses. Photograph: Royal Navy Museums

blocks.text: “When we look at the world now and we look at our military, it’s not about large set pieces – it’s often quite small incidents below the level of full-out declared wars. I think the medals ask questions about the world we live in now.”

Earlier this month, the Royal Marines returned to the Faroe Islands for the first time since the second world war as part of security efforts in the strategically vital Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap. This autumn, commando engineers have been practising digging underground hospitals that offer protection against drone attacks.

Sheldon said he thought the medals could prompt visitors to ask questions of themselves. “They are about a moment in time and somebody’s choice in that moment. They are powerful because they make you think: ‘What would I have done in the same incident.’”
Staff at the museum say it is hard to pick out a favourite story but when pressed, Sheldon said he was very keen on that of Sgt Norman Augustus Finch, born in 1890.
Finch was awarded the Victoria Cross during the Zeebrugge Raid on 23 April 1918. While serving onboard HMS Vindictive, Finch was stationed on a high lookout platform.

During the battle, his position was hit by shells, killing or wounding everyone around him. Although he was severely injured, Finch remained at his post and continued to fire on enemy positions until another shell finally put him out of action.

blocks.caption: L/Cpl Walter Richard Parker who served as a stretcher bearer during the Gallipoli campaign in May 1915.  Photograph: Royal Navy Museums

blocks.text: Because of the bravery shown by the entire battalion, the marines were allowed to vote for who should receive the VC. Finch was chosen by his peers.
Mark Berry, the assistant curator of artefacts, said he liked the story of L/Cpl Walter Richard Parker. During the Gallipoli campaign, Parker served as a stretcher bearer.

On the morning of 1 May 1915, Parker was a member of a party tasked with taking aid to men in an isolated frontline trench. To reach the trench, Parker crossed 365 metres (400 yards) of open ground under intense enemy fire.
He was the only person to successfully reach the trench. Having aided the wounded, he helped them evacuate the next morning, and himself was severely injured in the thigh and chest.
Berry said: “It’s a really good example of the multilayered role of the marines. It’s not just fighting. It’s also trying to save lives, trying to help people.”

items: The Royal Marines Experience opens at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard on 24 October.

articles.title: Starlink: How Elon Musk's company influences geopolitics
articles.summary: Designed to bring internet access to remote regions, Elon Musk's Starlink has become vital in crisis regions and war zones. But Ukraine also shows the risks of depending on the service.

image.caption: Starlink satellites have become vital means of communication in war zonesImage: Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Lack of internet access is a major problem in many regions of the world today.

Starlink was initially developed by the American tech billionaire Elon Musk to solve this problem. It was designed as a way of quickly getting the internet into regions all over the world where this was either impossible to do by conventional methods, or so expensive that it wasn't worth attempting.

blocks.caption: Starlink and SpaceX founder, controversial billionaire Elon MuskImage: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Since then, Starlink's field of application has widened significantly. It's used as a means of communication in disaster zones, but also by armies or protest movements, for example in regions where the existing internet has been destroyed by enemy fire or shut down by authoritarian governments.
But there is a downside: Ukraine's military, for example, is heavily dependent on Musk's satellite system. This has become especially apparent as the service faces external disruption.
How does Starlink work?

Starlink, which is operated by Musk's SpaceX company, is a satellite-based system consisting of 10,000 small satellites located around the world. They transfer data packages via laser links and do not require a constant, direct visual link to a ground station.

Unlike other internet satellites, which orbit at around 36,000 kilometers (22,000 miles) above the Earth, Starlink satellites are only about 550 kilometers up. This means they can transmit internet signals much faster than the others.

All users need is a small receiver terminal with an electronically controlled antenna, which automatically steers toward the satellites as they pass overhead. The terminals receive signals from these satellites and transmit them to a nearby router, which supplies the broadband internet connection.

blocks.caption: Starlink receivers smuggled into Iran enabled the opposition to organize despite the internet shutdownImage: Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Where has Starlink already been deployed?

Ukraine: Since the start of the Russia's full-scale war in February 2022, Starlink has become a vital instrument of communication in the war zone. The Ukrainian armed forces use Starlink to coordinate units, operate drones and control unmanned ground systems. In the civilian sector, the system is used by hospitals, emergency services, energy suppliers and the railway network.
Ukraine offers a particularly vivid example of how heavily its military capabilities now depend on Starlink.

In mid-October, Ukrainian army units reported disruptions to data transmission, which are said to have severely affected the control of combat, interceptor- and reconnaissance drones. Elon Musk said that restrictions on the speed and use of Starlink are determined by the US military and ultimately the US president. At this stage, it remains unclear who ordered the restrictions.

Iran: In early January 2026, protests erupted all across the country against the regime in Tehran. The government's hardline response included a nationwide internet shutdown. Reportedly, thousands of Starlink terminals were smuggled into Iran and sold on the black market. This enabled the protest movement to go on coordinating demonstrations against the regime, using Starlink to circumvent state censorship of the internet.
How reliable is Starlink as a wartime communications line?

The country's authorities are cracking down on the satellite service and its users. Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, the secretary of the Supreme Council of Cyberspace, described Starlink as a hostile "tool of war" and said the regime had means at its disposal to disrupt satellite connections.

Starlink is officially banned in Iran. Anyone using the service faces a prison sentence of six months to two years. If users are also charged with endangering national security or espionage, the offence can even carry the death penalty.

Sudan: In the Sudanese civil war, Starlink is used primarily by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group fighting against the internationally-recognized government. Hundreds of devices were smuggled into the country via the United Arab Emirates, and there is now a thriving black market for Starlink terminals in Sudan. The RSF use them to communicate and coordinate with their militias, while the Sudanese Armed Forces are trying to block both the import and use of the terminals.

Venezuela: Here too, Starlink has been used in the past to sidestep information blackouts and secure access to the internet. For a long time, the service was only available unofficially, by buying kits from local dealers. Following the US intervention in early January 2026, during which then-head of state, Nicolas Maduro, was taken prisoner, Musk offered the people of Venezuela a month's free broadband internet service via Starlink.

Gaza: Starlink has been used for humanitarian purposes in the devastated Gaza Strip since July 2024. Aid organizations and a field hospital use it to facilitate telemedical assistance and logistical coordination. Access for civilians remains limited because of Israeli security concerns.
Why has Starlink been criticized?

Starlink is often the only way to access the internet in conflict zones. This gives Musk and his operating company SpaceX tremendous influence. Previously, for example, Musk refused to activate Starlink in Ukraine to enable an attack in Crimea. US President Donald Trump has also threatened to switch off the satellites in Ukraine, as a way of forcing Kyiv to make concessions in peace negotiations.

blocks.caption: Starlink has provided vital communications for Ukrainian soldiers since the start of the 2022 Russian invasionImage: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance

blocks.text: There has also been criticism from an ecological perspective. The Starlink satellites have a lifespan of less than five years. Every day, on average, one or two of them burn up in the Earth's atmosphere. This releases aluminum oxide, which could affect the ozone layer, contributing to global warming. In addition, all those thousands of satellites reflect the sunlight, making the night sky brighter, and this may also have repercussions for the world's animals.
Any Starlink alternatives?

In an effort to break Starlink's monopoly, other companies, especially in Europe, are already working on alternatives. At present, the biggest private competitor to SpaceX is a company called Eutelsat. With a fleet of over 600 satellites, its OneWeb service is far smaller, focusing on business customers and maritime use.

But Eutelsat is also involved in the development of IRIS2 — an acronym for Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite, an ambitious EU project to establish a highly secure satellite network. The aim is to make Europe less dependent on Starlink, but IRIS2 won't be fully operational before 2032.

Elon Musk also has competition inside the US from another billionaire, Jeff Bezos, whose company Amazon is currently working on Amazon Leo, known until recently as Project Kuiper. This is establishing a network of more than 3,200 new low-Earth-orbit satellites. Amazon plans to roll out the service later this year in the US, Canada, France, Britain and Germany.

blocks.caption: Chinese competition for Starlink and SpaceX: The launch of a Chinese rocket carrying astronauts to a space station in April 2025Image: Andy Wong/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The sky is clearly getting crowded. China is also refining two satellite communications systems of its own. Guowang, a state project conceived primarily for national and military purposes, will consist of up to 13,000 satellites, while another project, Qianfan, with an estimated 12,000 satellites, is more commercially oriented and aims to provide services to newly industrialized and developing countries. The first mass starts for both of these projects are planned for this year.
Will Russia have its own Starlink?
This article has been translated from German.
Editor's note: This piece was originally published on February 14, 2026. It was updated on October 15, 2026, to reflect recent developments.

articles.title: Raul Daza, longtime congressman of Northern Samar, dies
articles.summary: Daza had been president of the Liberal Party and was, at the peak of his political career, the second-in-command in the House of Representatives

blocks.text: Statesman Raul Daza passes away at 91.
Daza had been president of the Liberal Party and was, at the peak of his political career, the second-in-command in the House of Representatives
MANILA, Philippines – Statesman Raul Daza, the longtime legislator from Northern Samar, has passed away, his family announced on Thursday, October 15.

“He peacefully passed away at 91 years old. He was a devoted husband, loving father, grandfather, great-grandfather, son, brother, colleague, mentor and friend,” read the statement of his widow Teresita Ruiz and their family.
“He leaves a legacy of integrity, courage, humility, empathy and commitment to democracy. He was a man who genuinely put himself in the shoes of others,” it added.

Daza served seven non-consecutive terms in the House of Representatives between 1969 and 2019, and was, at the peak of his political career, speaker pro tempore from 1992 to 1998. He was also governor of Northern Samar from 2001 to 2010.
He served as deputy minister of the Presidential Commission on Good Government, the agency tasked with going after the Marcos family’s ill-gotten wealth.

“A steadfast defender of democracy, justice, and the rule of law, he stood firm in his convictions through the Martial Law years and political exile. He was a member of the Liberal Party (LP) for 61 years, beginning in 1965, and served as its president from 1994 to 1998,” the family’s statement reads.
“Despite the many colors of politics, he firmly believed that we have only one flag and we have only one country,” it added.
Daza was a certified public accountant and a lawyer who graduated from the University of the Philippines College of Law. His family said he placed 11th in the Bar exam.
After retiring from politics in 2019, he was succeeded in Congress by his son, Paul, and later his grandson, Niko.
Details of his memorial are as follows:

items: October 17 to 19: 3 to 10 pm, The Chapels at Heritage Park, Taguig
October 18: 7 pm, Tribute by LP, The Chapels at Heritage Park, Taguig
October 19: 10 am to 12 pm, Necrological Service, House of Representatives, Batasan Hills, Quezon City
October 21 to 22: 1 pm (October 21) to 12 pm (October 22), Daza Residence in Daganas, Catarman, Northern Samar
October 22 to 24: 1 pm (October 22) to 12 pm (October 24), Provincial Capitol Gymnatorium, Dalakit, Catarman, Northern Samar
October 24: Funeral Mass at 1 pm, Our Lady of Annunciation Cathedral, Catarman, Northern Samar

articles.title: Texas resident discovers second world war-era grenades in box bought at estate sale
articles.summary:
Discovery of grenades prompted a neighborhood lockdown and a visit from the Austin police department’s bomb squad

A buyer at a Texas estate sale discovered several second world war-era…

blocks.text: A buyer at a Texas estate sale discovered several second world war-era grenades in a box of newly bought items, prompting a neighborhood lockdown and a visit from the Austin police department’s bomb squad.
The grenades, which were described as “live and active” in a social media post by the Austin police association, were removed and disarmed.
Their age and apparent volatility, the post said, required delicate handling by bomb squad members whose “training, expertise, and steady nerves” is rarely seen by the public.
“Handling 80-year-old explosives with unknown stability is dangerous, precise work, and they do it with the professionalism this city counts on,” the post said.
“Huge thanks to our patrol officers, who quickly secured the scene, set up a perimeter, and kept neighbors safe while they waited for EOD [explosive ordinance disposal].”

The police association did not identify the seller or buyer of the box of grenades, and said the person who bought them made the discovery only as he was rifling through several boxes of his new items on Monday.

“No crime here,” the post said. “Just a great reminder, if you ever come across old military ordnance (grenades, shells, mortar rounds, etc), even if you think it’s inert, don’t touch it, don’t move it, and call 911.
“Let the experts handle it.”

Austin’s KLBJ news station identified at least three of the olive-colored grenades as Mk 2 anti-personnel fragmentation grenades, widely used by US forces during the second world war, and known as “pineapple” grenades because of their distinctive shape.
The grenades were still in limited use with the US army and Marine Corps until the 1960s.
The station said bomb squad technicians examined the highly explosive devices with X-rays and determined they were live, but did not pose an immediate threat under the circumstances.

The Guardian reported earlier this month on the dangers specialist teams face in dealing with decades-old unexploded ordinance, including the degradation of fuses and increasing instability of explosives over time.

It followed the discovery of two large, unexploded German bombs found separately in the UK county of Devon, one on a floating dredger and another on a building site. Experts said the devices “could knock a whole street down”.

articles.title: Texas Democrat James Talarico faces grilling from voters at town hall in tight Senate race
articles.summary:
Talarico casts himself as a moderate who would put Texans’ needs over party allegiances amid close contest against Republican Ken Paxton

James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for…

blocks.text: James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, sat face to face with skeptical Republicans and independents voters who grilled him on a slew of contentious issues including Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, abortion and foreign aid, during a CNN town hall co-hosted by the Jubilee Media digital platform on Wednesday.

One voter, a young Republican activist who volunteered at the party’s midterm convention in Dallas last month and recently appeared on Fox News as a supporter of Talarico’s opponent, questioned the authenticity of Talarico’s faith, referencing a past remark where he described God as nonbinary.

“When I said that, I was being provocative and I want to admit that and come clean about that,” Talarico responded. “What I was saying is actually not controversial theologically: the idea that we can’t define God using human categories. Not only did I say that, but the late Charlie Kirk said that – the late Pope Benedict said that.”
Talarico added that he was receptive to feedback from Christians.

Jodi Hunt, a self-described single-issue voter, probed Talarico’s pro-choice stance, asking: “How would you convince me as a Catholic voter that I can trust you would protect the most innocent among us?”
Talarico described the Bible as being silent on abortion, to which Hunt countered quoting “Thou shalt not kill”.

“We may have different, moral conclusions when it comes to this particular ethical question, but we actually have the same public policy goal,” Talarico said, framing abortion as a public health issue that could be solved with a reduction in unplanned pregnancies.
During the night, Talarico cast himself as a moderate, who would put the needs of Texans over party allegiances. He railed against the ultra-wealthy, framing them as the common enemy.

Talarico and the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, are locked in a competitive race to become Texas’s next US senator, with most recent polls showing Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton. (Paxton declined an invitation to appear on CNN, host Erin Burnett said at the start of the town hall.)

Though Democrats have not won a Senate seat in the state since the late 1980s, they’re hoping Talarico’s newcomer energy and popular appeal will persuade independents and Republicans fed up with Donald Trump’s second term – or turned off by Paxton’s many scandals.

Over the weekend, Talarico became the subject of a disinformation campaign after he was absent from the campaign trail for more than a week. While Talarico’s campaign repeatedly said the candidate was sick with a bad case of the flu, conservative influencers falsely accused him of receiving medical treatment at a mental health facility in Ohio.
The rumor was further propelled by Paxton and Trump, who sought to fuel skepticism about Talarico’s health and fitness for office.
The Democratic candidate denied the false allegations after returning to the campaign trail last week, noting he had never been to Ohio.

“False claims got millions of views online and this is an example of what I call the ‘rage economy’,” Talarico said during the town hall. “Billionaires who own these platforms get rich. We all get angry and nobody’s life gets any better. Conspiracy theories don’t put food on the table, put gas in the tank, or improve our communities.”

Paxton, meanwhile, has been battling his own controversies. A series of leaked audio recordings – made during a closed-door meeting – have been posted online and revealed him being critical of his own party and campaign leaders in DC.

Paxton entered the race with a history of scandals. He was impeached by the Texas state legislature in 2023 on allegations including bribery and abuse of public trust, though he was later acquitted. Paxton’s wife of almost four decades, Angela Paxton, then filed for divorce in 2025 on “biblical grounds”, citing adultery.
But Trump endorsed Paxton to run against Talarico, passing up incumbent Republican John Cornyn.

articles.title: DOLE says AI not a threat but strategic opportunity
articles.summary: The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) said on Thursday that it is optimistic about artificial intelligence (AI), noting that it is not a threat but an opportunity to be treated responsibly.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 8:32pm
The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) said on Thursday that it is optimistic about artificial intelligence (AI), noting that it is not a threat but an opportunity to be treated responsibly.

“We in the Department of Labor and Employment view AI not as a threat to be feared but as a strategic opportunity to be harnessed responsibly,” said DOLE Monitoring and Evaluation Division chief Hannah Gale Perea during the HR&WorkTech Summit 2026 in Quezon City.
According to the World Economic Forum (WEF), literacy on AI and big data is the number one fastest-growing skill by 2030.

“AI enables our domestic industries to transition towards higher-value services, moving up the global value chain into areas such as AI system oversight, complex analytics, and high-tier technical support,” Perea said.
But in the same report by the WEF, analytical thinking is the top skill needed in the workplace in 2025.
For its part, DOLE said that management of AI exposure in the workplace dictates whether it will result in displacement or employment transformation.
“By augmenting human capability rather than simply replacing it, AI can increase overall productivity, elevate wage potential, and improve working conditions,” said Perea.

The Philippine digital economy reached a Gross Value Added (GVA) of P2.74 trillion in 2025, accounting for 9.8% of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) in April.
In 2025, the digital economy employed 10.39 million people, accounting for 21.2% of the country’s total workforce. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
articles.summary: Rescue officials fear more people are buried under the debris in the north-western city of Peshawar.
articles.byline: Bilal Ahmed and Azizullah Khan, Phelan Chatterjee

blocks.text: At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.
More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition. Several children are feared to be trapped under the rubble.
Emergency services were alerted to the incident at the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, a rescue official said.
He told the BBC the roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, causing ceilings below to cave in as well.
Warning: This article contains distressing details
"The children in the affected [classrooms] were trapped under the debris," the official, Bilal Faizi, said.
The school is located in a building that had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak.

Earlier reports suggested the affected classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down. There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.
It appears that when the roof of the upper-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.
Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.

Angie de Silva/Rappler
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa joins WNYC's Brian Lehrer for a live conversation on defending and rebuilding democracy in the age of artificial intelligence

MANILA, Philippines – Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa will join WNYC host Brian Lehrer for a conversation on democracy in the age of artificial intelligence (AI) on Thursday, October 15, in New York (Friday, October 16, Philippine time).
The event, “Democracy Dialogues,” is co-presented by New York Public Radio (NYPR) and Rappler and will take place at The Greene Space in Lower Manhattan.

Lehrer, host of the Peabody Award-winning The Brian Lehrer Show, and Ressa will discuss the challenges of understanding, defending, and rebuilding democracy at a time when AI is rapidly transforming how people access information and engage with the world.
“Democracy Dialogues” is NYPR’s ongoing live event series examining the state of democracy and the roles of journalism, free expression, and an informed public in sustaining democratic institutions.
The conversation comes as Ressa releases her new book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators, on October 13.

The event will also be livestreamed on WNYC’s website, C-SPAN, and on Rappler’s YouTube channel. Portions of the conversation will air on The Brian Lehrer Show on Friday, October 16, at 10 am Eastern Time.

articles.title: Should you upgrade to the iPhone 18 Pro Max?
articles.summary: After unboxing our early access to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, we were able to make some conclusions. Are you looking for a better camera? If your answer is yes then know that Apple has completely…

blocks.text: After unboxing our early access to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, we were able to make some conclusions.
Are you looking for a better camera?

If your answer is yes then know that Apple has completely re-engineered the main camera of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max with a variable aperture. If you zoom in on the main lens you can actually see the opening move to adjust how much light comes in. You can go from the widest f/1.48 for very low light areas to f/4.0 for wider shots.
Are you a professional creative who needs to secure copyright?

If you are a creative professional, Apple has also introduced Reference Image on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Whenever you take a photo, your phone stamps a cryptographic identifier to the photo which is like the equivalent of a digital negative. This is useful in the age of AI and social media where one needs to prove that an image was taken by the original creator and prove copyright.
Are you looking to use this without a case?

Although it may look very similar on the outside, the new Pro and Pro Max have a different layout on the vapor chamber where the A20 chip and RAM are not sandwiched on top of one another, but placed side by side. This allows for better cooling in the vapor chamber. Previous models would heat up by the camera plateau but this has been vastly improved – yes there’s still heat build up but significantly less now. That means you can use the new iPhones with those minimalist case brackets.

blocks.caption: iPhone 18 Pro Max Unit in Silver

blocks.text: That being said, the new iPhone 18 Pro Max has the exact same button configuration as the previous model which means your old cases will work fine!

If money is no object and you’re willing to upgrade anyway, you can always give your old iPhone to your child. That also means that for parents, iOS 27 has completely revamped the parental controls onboarding, making it easier to monitor your kid’s Internet behavior on iOS or iPad OS. Simply reset your old phone, say you’re setting up the iPhone for your child, and follow the on-screen instructions.

blocks.caption: iPhone 18 Pro Max camera module

blocks.text: Other than improved battery life if you find these reasons compelling enough to get you to upgrade, the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are launching at midnight with many store promos from official stores so you don’t get scammed!

articles.title: Severe drought declared in six areas of England as public water supplies under threat
articles.summary:
Some reservoirs in south-east and south-west at critically low levels as water companies call for non-essential user bans on businesses

A severe drought has been declared in six areas of…

blocks.text: A severe drought has been declared in six areas of England with some reservoirs at critically low levels, threatening public supplies.
Parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex have moved into severe drought, and urgent measures are being taken to secure public supplies of water.

Despite the crisis, the environment secretary Angela Eagle has yet to approve requests from three water companies, in areas now in severe drought, to extend restrictions on water use to businesses such as golf clubs and commercial car washes.
Emma Hardy, the water minister, indicated on Thursday that the environment could suffer in the ongoing drought.

Hardy instructed the Environment Agency to prioritise protecting public water supplies in areas affected by severe drought where there is an unavoidable trade-off between environmental rules and water supplies.
After a meeting of the national drought group, Eagle, said: “This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades, so this government is stepping up our support and planning.
“We are working closely with water companies to protect public supplies in the areas affected, and I’d continue to urge everyone to think about how they can use water wisely over the coming weeks.”

South East Water, South West Water and Southern Water want to impose non-essential user bans on businesses to protect supplies. This would affect golf clubs, private schools and commercial properties. But while Eagle called on water companies to step up their drought planning, she did not announce approval for the non-essential user bans.
The south-east and south-west of England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century, fuelled by the climate crisis, affecting reservoir levels in those areas.
Levels at two reservoirs are critically low. Ardingly reservoir, which serves about 95,000 properties in Haywards Heath, Uckfield and surrounding areas, is only 19% full.
Storage at Wimbleball, which supplies South West Water customers in East Devon, North Devon, Somerset and West Dorset and Wessex Water customers in West Somerset, is at 16%.
The Environment Agency would expect reservoir storage to be about 75% for this time of year.

There are also concerns for several smaller South West Water reservoirs serving homes in Devon and Cornwall; these include Drift and Stithians which supply 56,000 households in Cornwall, and the Tottiford and Venford group which supplies 47,000 households in Devon.

The National Drought Group said the government and the Environment Agency would move to daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels and run heightened water quality monitoring because of the lower dilution levels of sewage, raising the risks for water quality and environmental pollution.
Businesses that abstract water will be put through more compliance checks to make sure they are taking only what they are allowed.

Philip Duffy, the chief executive of the EA, said: “We cannot change the weather, but water companies can act now. We expect them to follow their drought plans and take the steps needed to secure public water supplies.
“We are also asking everyone to use less water. That will leave more in our rivers and the environment, helping farmers and protecting wildlife and nature.”

articles.title: Hypersonic missiles highlight arms race on Korean Peninsula
articles.summary: Both South and North Korea have tested weapons feared by military planners for their speed and ability to maneuver in flight.

image.caption: Hypersonic missiles are far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy [FILE: January 6, 2022]Image: YONHAPNEWS AGENCY/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea announced that it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on Wednesday — a day after the state-run Korean Central News Agency reported that leader Kim Jong Un had visited a new defense industry museum, where he admired an intercontinental ballistic missile reportedly capable of hitting targets in the continental United States.
The visit came five days after South Korean President Lee Jae-myung observed the test launch of his country's first domestically developed hypersonic missile.

South Korea's breakthrough came after Pyongyang announced a test on October 3 of what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that traveled 350 kilometers (220 miles) before striking its target.

"Comrade Kim Jong Un expressed the expectation and belief that all the nation's missile forces would remain faithful to their missions of defending the sovereignty and security of the republic in a responsible combat posture," the KCNA reported.
'Advanced conventional weapons'
Both North and South Korea are primarily racing to develop hypersonic technology because it offers a step-up in offensive capabilities at a time of worsening tensions in the Indo-Pacific region.

blocks.caption: Pyongyang said it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on October 14Image: KCNA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Hypersonic missiles are weapons that can travel at velocities of at least five times the speed of sound (Mach 5) or over 6,100 kilometers per hour.

Their speed makes it far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy inbound missiles, which can carry conventional or nuclear warheads. Their additional advantage over previous generations of missiles is their ability to suddenly change course, dip or weave in flight, making interception significantly more difficult.

"There has been an arms race on the Korean Peninsula for many years and hypersonic weapons are just the latest manifestation of that," said Chris Green, Korea Peninsula analyst for Crisis Group International.
Hypersonic weapons have become a "priority for the South" as the North has ramped up its capabilities and forged military and economic ties with Russia, he said.
"And North Korea has nuclear weapons, but it would not be viable to use them as the threat has always been that doing so would mean that the US would turn the country to glass," he told DW.
"For the North, it is unsurprising that the geopolitics of the region have encouraged them to pursue advanced conventional weapons as they try to have dominance on the peninsula."
What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war?
Pyongyang 'should not be underestimated'

And while it is impossible to confirm with any certainty that the weapons the North says it has developed have the capabilities they claim, Green said it would be a mistake to underestimate Pyongyang.

"We do not know their capabilities and it is possible this is all propaganda, but there is a long list of times the North's capabilities have been underestimated only to be shown that they can, in fact, do what they say."
Chun In-bum, a retired general in the South Korean army and now a senior fellow with the National Institute for Deterrence Studies, shares that assessment of the threat.
"It's anybody's guess whether they're telling the truth on this, but any prudent military planner should always assume the worst," he said.
The North's mastery of the advanced technology required to operate hypersonic missiles appears to have been sudden, although it remains unclear how it acquired the capability.

"They probably obtained the technology through illegal means," Chun said. "They snoop around firms in the US, South Korea and Japan for this sort of information, but they also do it to their 'friends.'"
Wherever the data came from, the fact that North Korea's hypersonic missiles appear to have performed as required should be cause for deep concern.

"A greater offensive capability increases the overall danger posed by the North, and if they have weapons that are harder to shoot down, then it is possible there are greater temptations to use them," Chun said.
"I'm speculating, of course, but I'm sure that we are looking at ways to neutralize this particular threat, but as I understand it there is no good answer right now," Chun added.
South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North
Canceling each other out?
Green, however, believes that both sides developing viable systems means that they may cancel each other out as a potent battlefield advantage.

"I do not think this changes the balance of power," he said. "The North still has its nuclear deterrent and this 'porcupine strategy' of being sharp and prickly in order to keep everyone else at arm's length. And it's not a game changer south of the Demilitarized Zone either," the expert added.

"It is clear, however, that if the North continues to develop its offensive systems and is able to deploy them in huge numbers, then there will have to be a conversation about greater missile defense not only in the South but also in Japan, and that will then raise some very difficult questions."

articles.title: Métis leaders in oilsands region say they haven’t been consulted on proposed Pacific Link pipeline
articles.summary: Métis leaders in the Fort McMurray region say Prime Minister Mark Carney has not met with them to discuss the proposed Pacific Link pipeline, despite meeting with the chiefs of nearby First Nations.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, flanked by Pembina Pipeline CEO Scott Burrows and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, at a press conference north of Fort McMurray, Alta., announcing next steps to accelerate the West Coast pipeline project. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton
Métis leaders in the Fort McMurray region say Prime Minister Mark Carney has not met with them to discuss the proposed Pacific Link pipeline, despite meeting with the chiefs of nearby First Nations.
Métis leaders raised concerns at news conference in Fort McMurray
Métis leaders in Alberta’s Wood Buffalo region are accusing the federal government of excluding them from discussions on the proposed Pacific Link pipeline project.

Before announcing earlier this month that the new West Coast oil pipeline would be designated as being in the national interest under the Building Canada Act, Prime Minister Mark Carney met with several First Nations leaders about the issue. But the leaders of six Métis communities say he never met with them to discuss the proposed pipeline before announcing it.

At a news conference held in Fort McMurray, Alta., on Tuesday, Métis leaders noted they were also not invited to the joint federal-provincial news conference for the pipeline announcement on Oct. 1, and were not told about ownership stakes for the project.
“Silence is acceptance and that’s why we’re not silent,” Kelly Myers, district captain for Fort McMurray Métis, told reporters.

“Based on the fact that there were so many others that were invited to this announcement and we were not clearly shows a sign of disrespect to Métis as a whole, and it’s one that we’re just not going to accept.”
CBC News contacted the federal government’s Privy Council Office for comment but had yet to receive a response at the time of publication.

Leaders from six Métis communities in the Fort McMurray Wood Buffalo region pose for a photo at the Quality Inn Hotel in Fort McMurray on Oct. 13, 2026. From left: Councillors Lana Huppie and Brenda Paquette of Fort McKay Métis Nation; Loretta Waquan, president of Fort McKay Métis Nation; Paul Tremblay, vice-president of Conklin Métis Local 193; Ruby Ladouceur, president of Fort Chipewyan Métis Nation; Stella Lavallee, president of Willow Lake Métis Nation; Kelly Myers, district captain for Fort McMurray Métis; Jennifer Vardy, strategist with Chard Métis Nation. (Image supplied by McMurray Métis)

If approved, the proposed Pacific Link pipeline will carry one million barrels of oil per day from Alberta’s oilsands region to tankers at a deepwater port near Delta, B.C. The federal government and Alberta’s provincial government hope to have approvals for construction by September 2027 and to have the pipeline operational by 2032 or 2033.
Carney has said a 10 per cent ownership stake will be available for Indigenous communities. The federal government says there will also be Indigenous contracting and employment opportunities.

“We’re developing this pipeline with Indigenous peoples involved from the start,” Carney said during his announcement on Oct. 1. “This is the start of that development with the opportunities to share in the prosperity that Pacific Link will create.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney announces the Pacific Link pipeline project during a visit to Fort McMurray, Alta., on Oct. 1, 2026. (Emilio Avalos/CBC/Radio-Canada)
The Métis leaders who say they were not consulted about the project represent communities in Fort McMurray, Fort Chipewyan, Fort McKay, Willow Lake, Conklin and Chard.

At Tuesday’s news conference, none of them said they opposed the pipeline, but in a statement and media scrum, they said they have concerns and questions that they want to raise before any federal approvals are signed.

Ruby Ladouceur, president of Fort Chipewyan Métis Nation, said she believes the pipeline will lead to more oilsands development. Premier Danielle Smith has previously said she wants oilsands production to double to eight million barrels per day by 2035.
Ladouceur said she worries that increased production will increase the risk of accidents that could have environmental impacts on water, land and the air.
“Anything done without us is actually against us,” said Ladouceur, who also pointed out that Carney met with First Nations chiefs on National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

“They didn’t consult with us, they didn’t even let us know about anything that was taking place about the pipeline and it goes through our region,” said Stella Lavallee, president of Willow Lake Métis Nation.

items: Mayors, First Nations chiefs in Alberta's oilsands region react tentatively to West Coast pipeline designation
Water, toxic waste and opportunity: Indigenous leaders react to Carney's pipeline plan

blocks.text: Zoe De Jonge, press secretary for Alberta Indigenous Relations Minister Rajan Sawhney, told CBC News in an email that the ministry has been meeting with Indigenous leaders about the project. She said the province could not comment on any engagement decisions made by the federal government.
“Our commitment to engaging with First Nations and Métis communities remains a priority for Alberta’s government,” said De Jonge.

“Minister Sawhney has met with Métis leaders and communities across the Fort McMurray Wood Buffalo region, and remains committed to maintaining those relationships through continued dialogue and engagement.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Vincent McDermott covers Fort McMurray and the Wood Buffalo region for CBC News. He was previously the editor of Fort McMurray Today, where he was part of a team that won a National Newspaper Award for coverage of the 2016 Horse River Wildfire. He is also a former contributor to the official magazine of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada. He can be reached at vincent.mcdermott@cbc.ca

articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries as Zelenskyy says 'we're done'
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has announced that Ukraine is resuming attacks on Russian energy sites. It came after Moscow summarily ignored a claim by US President Donald Trump that an "energy ceasefire" had…

image.caption: Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian refineries after Russia fails to observe US 'truce'Image: EyePress News/Newscom/IMAGO

blocks.text: Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Thursday said that his country's military had resumed strikes on Russian energy infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump's insistence that such attacks stop.
Zelenskyy made the statement in an interview with London's Financial Times (FT) newspaper, saying: "The block [on energy infrastructure attacks] is out. We're done."
The announcement came after Russia reported Ukrainian attacks on oil processing plants in Ryazan, where fire broke out, and Saratov.
Kyiv had refrained from making attacks to give Trump's "energy ceasefire" a chance for success.

On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised "vigorous [US] efforts to initiate the peace process," and claimed that by resuming attacks, Ukraine "is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators."

Russia, however, has paid no heed to Trump, instead continuing to hit Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure, for instance on Wednesday, when Russian strikes cut power to 600,000 Ukrainian citizens.

blocks.caption: Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Trump's 'ceasefire' on energy sites: 'We're done'Image: Dan Bashakov/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kyiv's blasts dangerous lack of US intel
Ukraine had gone along with Trump's public proposal — despite not being notified of any "ceasefire" ahead of time — but it seemed to have helped little in the eyes of US leadership.

To that end, Zelenskyy railed against a "dangerous" lack of US intelligence information this week as well as the throttling of SpaceX Starlink satellite access for Ukraine's troops after Trump last week announced a number of decisions that have had adverse consequences for Ukraine.
The Ukrainian president said his country's military leaders had been warned that they would not be receiving US intelligence if they did not abide by Trump's "ceasefire."
Ukraine: Russian strikes continue as ceasefire questions remain
Despite Ukraine's restraint, that withholding of intelligence was on full display this week when Kyiv was blindsided by Russian drones and missiles without any prior warning from the US.
"We will find a way out," said Zelenskyy of the situation as Ukraine's Western allies scramble to pick up the intelligence and defensive slack left by the US.

Zelenskyy said he would be willing to halt energy infrastructure attacks again but only if the US supplied Patriot interceptors that would allow Kyiv to down incoming the Russian ballistic missiles and drones that have been raining down on Ukraine since February 24, 2022.
Zelenskyy: Starlink throttling a question of US 'will'
Despite US claims that the Starlink situation was the result of a technical glitch, Zelenskyy told the FT, "It was not a technical problem, it was will."
SpaceX owner Elon Musk said the US owns and operates the Starshield military version of Starlink used by Ukraine, adding that he and his company had nothing to do with the issue.
Ukraine presses allies on intelligence sharing

The FT interview comes in the wake of Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil as well as his promise to buy "millions of barrels" of Russian diesel fuel amid high fuel prices caused by the US war with Iran.

The deal, just weeks from the US midterm elections, is unlikely to bring down oil prices. But it does extend a lifeline to Russian President Putin, allowing him to continue his illegal invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy and went so far as to call for him to be replaced this weekend.
Trump's sanctions actions fly in the face of nearly five years of allied political efforts to pressure Moscow to end its invasion.
Trump's actions have enraged NATO allies and European leaders, with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, for one, calling the US agreement to purchase Russian diesel "a very risky decision."

Meloni pointed out that the spike in oil prices was clearly precipitated by Trump's war in Iran and that his dealings with Putin would result in the Russian leader continuing his invasion of Ukraine rather than ending it.

articles.title: Romania: 2 ships on fire in Black Sea, 7 crew missing
articles.summary: Two chemical tankers have caught fire in Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea. The blazes occurred after Russian drones were sighted in Romanian airspace.

image.caption: Several crew members from the Wine Trader are missing after a fire broke out onboardImage: Romanian Interior Ministry/REUTERS

blocks.text: Romanian authorities have launched search and rescue operations in the Black Sea in a bid to find seven missing crew from a chemical tanker that caught fire overnight to Thursday.
Another vessel, also a chemical tanker, was also set on fire in the same region some hours earlier, but all its crew is said to be safe.
The fires occurred after Russian drones strayed into Romanian airspace, though Romanian officials have so far not explicitly said the unmanned aircraft caused the blazes.

However, there have been drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships off the coasts of Romanian and neighboring Bulgaria — both NATO members — in the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors lost in those incidents.
What do we know about the ship fires in the Black Sea?
Both ships were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina Canal leading ‌to the Black Sea out of the Danube River when they caught fire.
Romania's naval authority said it launched its search and rescue operation after receiving an emergency alert ‌from ​the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader.
Five of the 12 crew members were said to be safe, while seven were missing.
"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," Defense Minister Radu Miruta told the Digi24 television channel.
"This is a matter of significant gravity, given that such incidents are occurring in Romanian territorial waters," he said.
The other fire, which broke out earlier, occurred onboard the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J.
Ships often use the canal as a place to anchor in the case of delays caused by weather or congestion.
Growing attacks in the Black Sea

Romania, which shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, has ⁠reported ​repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over ​the past four years during Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
The Danube and its ports are now frequently used by Ukrainian vessels as Ukraine's Black Sea ports come under attack from Russian forces.
Ukrainian ships are also choosing routes in the Black Sea close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.
This comes as shipping in the Black Sea has come under increasing attacks ​⁠in recent months that have drastically reduced grain transports from both Ukraine and Russia, both major cereal exporters.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Thursday that the EU, of which both his country and Romania are members, will discuss a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea at its ongoing summit in Brussels.
Bulgaria summoned the Russian ambassador over the sinking of a ship off the country's coast on Tuesday following a drone attack.

articles.title: UP Diliman students evacuate 2 school buildings after alleged threat
articles.summary: Students, faculty, and staff at two school buildings in the University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman campus in Quezon City were evacuated Thursday afternoon due to an alleged security threat.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 7:22pm
Students, faculty, and staff at two school buildings in the University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman campus in Quezon City were evacuated Thursday afternoon due to an alleged security threat.
According to a report by Tinig ng Plaridel, the student publication in UP Diliman College of Mass Communication, evacuation measures were implemented at Palma Hall and Malcolm Hall.
Images posted by Tinig ng Plaridel showed police responders clad in black combat gear speaking with a security guard on the Palma Hall steps.
A vehicle of the Quezon City (QC) Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (DRRMO) was parked nearby as students walked down the stairs.

The report quoted the UP Office of the Vice Chancellor for Community Affairs (OVCCA) as confirming the presence of personnel from QC DRRMO and the QC Police District's Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit to investigate the incident.
Youscooper Dawson Quiambao documented the exit of students at Palma Hall past 2 p.m.
According to a report by Isa Avendano-Umali on Super Radyo dzBB, a threat was posted on social media, which stated: "Maghahasik ng lagim sa buong Palma at Malcolm. Humanda kayong lahat."
(Horror will be unleashed all over Palma and Malcom. All of you be ready.)
Palma Hall, also known the College of Social Sciences and Philosophy (CSSP), is a major convergence point in the UP Diliman campus as courses of various disciplines are taught there.
On the other hand, Malcolm Hall is the UP College of Law.
The radio report added that the QCPD Explosive Ordnance Disposal team and school officials immediately responded by initiating inspections and safety procedures.
Authorities did not find any suspicious or hazardous items, the report said.
The QCPD was quoted as saying that investigation was still ongoing. The situation in the two buildings went back to normal as of posting time.

GMA News Online's calls to OVCCA phone numbers were unanswered. GMA News Online likewise reached out to the QC DRRMO but it has yet to respond as of this post. For its part, the QCPD said it would issue a statement at a later time. — VDV, GMA News

A graduate of Davao Doctors College Inc. scored the highest grade in the recent computer-based licensure examination, the Professional Regulation Commission said.
According to the PRC, 394 test takers out of 423 passed the exam, given by the Board of Optometry in Metro Manila in September (written) and October (practical).

Gabriell Jace Mart Legaspi Tangaran of Davao Doctor College achieved the top score of 92.11%, while the best-performing school with 50 or more test takers is Centro Escolar University-Manila, with 160 of its 169 examinees passing.

Among schools with 25 to 49 examinees, three had 100% passing rates: South western University (49 test takers), Manila Central University-Caloocan City (43) and Mindanao Medical Foundation College (30).
